analysis.one_liner: Cuts off all federal money for the Affordable Care Act and cancels its benefits and payments.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut off all federal funding for the Affordable Care Act was introduced in the House in July 2013 but never received a hearing or a vote in any committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have prohibited any federal money from being spent to carry out the Affordable Care Act — the 2010 law that created the health insurance marketplaces, expanded Medicaid, and protects people with pre-existing conditions [S2][S3]. It would have canceled every entitlement to ACA benefits, barred payments owed to states, and rescinded unspent ACA funds the day it took effect [S2][S3]. It was referred to six House committees and their subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing or vote for the rest of the Congress [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the people who gain would be those opposed to the ACA's expansion of government health programs — the bill would end federal spending on the law's programs, cancel payments owed to states, and rescind unspent funds [S2][S3]. No provision in the bill creates a replacement or transition for the people who would lose coverage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Opponents of the Affordable Care Act

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits any federal funds from being spent on carrying out the Affordable Care Act and the health provisions of the 2010 reconciliation act, and cancels any entitlement to benefits under those laws.
It bars payments owed to states and rescinds unobligated balances, cutting off ACA-related federal spending immediately rather than phasing it out.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on the millions of people who get coverage through the ACA's marketplaces and Medicaid expansion, since their benefits and subsidies would end outright [S2][S3]. States would also lose federal payments they were owed or expecting under the law [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: ACA enrollees and the states serving them

drawbacks.text: The bill would end Medicaid expansion funding and tax credits that help millions of low- and middle-income people afford insurance, leaving them without coverage unless Congress passed a replacement.
It would strip away protections such as the ban on denying coverage for pre-existing conditions, which depend on the ACA's funding and benefit structure.
It cancels payments already owed to states and rescinds unobligated funds immediately, which would uproot state insurance marketplaces and programs with no transition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: As written, the bill had large drawbacks: it would have stripped health coverage and subsidies from millions of people with no replacement, ended protections for pre-existing conditions, and raised costs for older and sicker enrollees. Because it died in committee without a vote or a hearing, no one bore those costs, and its failure preserved the ACA's benefits. Any benefit of the bill — lower federal spending on ACA programs — would have come at the direct expense of the people losing coverage.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to several House committees and their subcommittees in July 2013, and none of them ever took it up or voted on it before the session ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 11, 2013 and referred to six House committees, including Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and the Judiciary.
Within days it was referred to subcommittees, including the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, where the action history ends.
No committee ever reported the bill, no vote was ever taken on it in the House, and the Congress ended without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on ACA coverage and subsidies kept them; the bill died quietly without costing anyone a vote. Insurers and states that built programs on ACA funding were also spared the disruption it would have caused.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People keeping ACA coverage and subsidies

for.name: Rep. Tom Graves
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit all federal funding of the Affordable Care Act.

sides.party_line_note: All 158 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill, and no Democrat or any other member acted against it in the record because it never advanced to a vote.

industries.note: Defunding the ACA would end the premium subsidies and Medicaid expansion that channel federal money to private insurers and created their new individual-market customer base, but it would also erase the coverage expansion that brought insurers millions of newly insured, subsidized enrollees.
States running ACA marketplaces and the Medicaid expansion would lose federal payments and funding they had built programs around, with obligations already owed canceled outright.

industries.industry: Employers who already provide generous health benefits
industries.note: The bill would repeal the ACA's requirements and funding mechanisms that reshaped the employer insurance market, removing compliance costs for large incumbent employers.
